articleTitle: The pioneering years: the broadcasters perspective
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on UK Broadcast Manufactuerers - The Pioneering Years (Digest No: 1997/106)
abstract: The BBC had re-started the TV service in 1948 and had no option but to pick up the pieces of the pre-war installation, and work very hard to bring it up to date, and set a course for engineering excellence for the future. This is an important point in the context of an analysis of the "pioneering years". The policy of the BBC in respect of TV engineering development (and research into future technologies) has been to see this as a very important part of their role as state broadcasters. As a result, they devoted significant resources to this end, and played a major role in keeping British TV engineering in a prominent position in global TV technology.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on UK Broadcast Manufactuerers - The Pioneering Years (Digest No: 1997/106)
abstract: Digital television techniques have been with us for almost 30 years and commercially available digital television sub-systems were introduced almost 25 years ago. One of the first suppliers of such products was Quantel, formed in 1973. Not the very first to deliver digitally based equipment but the only survivor from the early seventies whose entire business depends solely on digital television and image processing equipment and which has survived the take-overs and mergers. It is that focus on digital television and digital images which has sustained continuous development of a wide range of applications, and created growth not by acquisition as is often the case today, but simply as a result of the volume of business. The Quantel product range has evolved through concentration on innovative solutions to customers needs rather than marketing analysis driven designs. This paper concentrates on the first 15 years or so focusing on the technology, some important product milestones and most importantly the personalities without whom the name Quantel may never have existed.

IEE Colloquium on UK Broadcast Manufactuerers - The Pioneering Years (Digest No: 1997/106)
abstract: Discusses the history of Cintel from its early days in the late 1920s when it was known as Baird Television Ltd. Baird Television Ltd. went into receivership in the late 1930s. 1940 saw the start up of Cinema Television Ltd. (from which the Cintel name is derived). The evolution of this company is then discussed upto the present. Some of the landmark technological achievements are mentioned.

articleTitle: Snell & Wilcox-81 years of collective experience
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on UK Broadcast Manufactuerers - The Pioneering Years (Digest No: 1997/106)
abstract: The Snell & Wilcox Group in the mid 1990s is a far cry from what it was 10 years ago. With the fusion of the original Snell and Wilcox, Electrocraft Consultants, and CEL, the Snell and Wilcox Group boasts a total of 81 company-years of video equipment experience (including digital image processors, standards convertors and TV equipment). The author discusses the evolution of the Snell & Wilcox Group through its constituent companies from the 1960s to the present.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on UK Broadcast Manufactuerers - The Pioneering Years (Digest No: 1997/106)
abstract: The author covers Marconi's contribution to radio and TV broadcasting equipment manufacturing industry during the post war period. He concentrates on television, somewhat to the detriment of radio, and in particular on television cameras, as in the days when everything was analogue, cameras were the most important product.

articleTitle: The Television Transmission Division of Pye
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on UK Broadcast Manufactuerers - The Pioneering Years (Digest No: 1997/106)
abstract: The Television Transmission Division of Pye played a major pioneering role in developing and manufacturing equipment for broadcasters both in the UK and abroad. The history of the operation is inevitably linked to the strategy and fortunes of the Pye company itself which was established by C. O. Stanley before the Second World War. With the knowledge and expertise gained from wartime developments the Television Transmission Division was formed and began working on cameras and ancillary equipment. As the business grew transmitters were developed and demonstrations of television, together with the Pye receiver activity, were made around the world. With the coming of ITV the company became a major supplier and in the UK projects were carried out for both the BBC, the ITA, and IBA. As the UK market became more mature after the introduction of colour the company, now called Pye TVT, moved towards an export led business. A troubled parent company was rescued by the Dutch giant Philips who proceeded to integrate its activities with those of Pye. In the 1970s Pye TVT became known as the Broadcast Company of Philips and the studio business was linked to the Philips' activities in Holland and the USA. By the middle of the 1980s Philips decided to concentrate its broadcast activities on the continent and the studio activity was closed, shortly after which Philips sold the transmitter activity. This paper tells the story of the company from its early tentative days to it becoming one of the world's major suppliers.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on UK Broadcast Manufactuerers - The Pioneering Years (Digest No: 1997/106)
abstract: Describes the development of some of the smaller companies that have figured in the development of UK TV broadcasting in the 1960s and 1970s. The author first gives a general view of markets, finance, training, staffing, international sales and the advent of Japanese companies. He goes on to discuss in more detail: Link Electronics Ltd., Michael Cox Electronics Ltd., Prowest Electronics Ltd., and Aston Electronic Designs Ltd.

articleTitle: The EMI story-the first and the greatest
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on UK Broadcast Manufactuerers - The Pioneering Years (Digest No: 1997/106)
abstract: By 1930, the His Masters Voice (HMV) Company had developed in their laboratories at Hayes a technique for mass printing of films on to paper stock and projecting them in a domestic episcope. However, in about 1930 the Company abandoned its short interest in making films. Early 1931, HMV and Columbia merged to form Electrical and Musical Industries (EMI). HMV had just completed its Abbey Road studios and the Columbia moving coil system was used to equip them. Work on television continued after the merger, based on converting the 150-line equipment to a 120-line 25 frame mirror-drum film scanner for transmission and a cathode-ray tube receiver. It was at this time that the system-design problems which would have to be solved if a worthwhile domestic entertainment service were to be set up began to emerge.
